# Tab 1

# Part 1: User Interface Mockups and Analysis.

### Wireframes-

![UI Wireframes](HW3Wireframes.png)

For our app, Hey There\!, we decided to focus on simplicity as our key design choice. This as a whole would make our app reliable and easy to follow; and with the addition of labelling almost everything, users will have a better time using our app. Additionally, we stuck to 6 main screens for our app: Create Account, Log In/Welcome Back, Profile Page, Location Settings, Messages and Map. With these 6 screens, users won’t have to scramble through multiple menus or tabs, just to find a certain feature. Now, with these simple wireframes, we can now transform them into functional UI applications.

### UI Prototypes-

![][image2]  
![][image3]

### Create Account-

For the Create Account page, it is a standard account creation page that any user may see online. It first shows our logo that we designed, a simple hand that is waving; signifying someone saying hello to you; followed by our software’s name “Hey There\!” Next, it asks users to create their account, followed by an input section for both email and password. Finally, it ends with the button to create an account, after you have imputed your email and password. Additionally, there is a standard link that would take you to the Log In page if you already have an account; it is placed directly under the create account button. Overall, this page is very simple and follows similar formatted account creation pages that users may have already seen before.

### Log In-

For the Log In page, it appears similarly  to the Create Account page, with a few changes. The Log In page also features the logo and the “Hey There\!”, but instead welcomes back the user as opposed to telling them to create an account. Next it follows the same format of email and password to log into the account and has a Log In button placed below to of course log in. Lastly, there is also a link underneath the log in button, that will take the user to the Create Account page if they do not already have an account; this acts similarly to the link the Create Account page has. Overall, this page is designed again very similarly to any Log In pages that users may have seen before, keeping it consistent. 

### Profile Page-

After creating an account or logging in; the user will be met at their Profile page to create their profile. This profile page is located on the tab at the bottom of the page to access, along with the other 3 major tabs that we will discuss soon. On the Profile page, users will be allowed to create/change their display name, bio, age, and add any interests they may have. For display name and bio, they each are simple input sections for users to type out said inputs. For age, we utilized a slider for users to choose their age. Lastly, for interests, users will be allowed to search for interests and choose from a variety available to them. When a user selects an interest, it will be highlighted for them and any interests that aren’t selected will be grayed out. Moreover, all changes made will be saved automatically. Overall, this page is simple and easy to understand/navigate as everything is clearly labeled and doesn’t provide any further instructions or clarifications to use; allowing users to easily customize their profiles.

### Settings-

For the Settings page, this holds all the settings needed to run the application on a location basis. The features this page holds are Location Broadcasting, Precise Location, Blackout Zones and the Log Out button. For location broadcasting, it is under Broadcast My Location and explains to the user what this setting does in simple terms. When turned on, it will broadcast the user’s location, and when turned off it will not. And to turn the setting on or off, it will utilize a button switch; when lit up, it signifies the setting is on, and when grayed out, it is signified as off; for the setting in the prototype, it is switched to on. Next, for precise location, it is under Use Precise Location and explains to the user what this setting does in simple terms. When turned on, the app will use your exact GPS location, but when switched off it will instead use a broad estimate. Moreover, just like with location broadcasting, this setting also uses a button switch and works the same way. For this setting in the prototype, it is switched to off. Next is blackout zones and explains to the user what this setting does in simple terms. A blackout zone will automatically turn off the user’s location when inside said zone, and the user can only have a max of 3 zones. To add these zones, the user will simply type an address or name of a place to act as a blackout zone; and after entering a valid location, they may click the plus icon to add it and will be displayed below; and to remove a certain zone, they can press the X icon to remove it. Finally, the log out button simply allows the user to log out of their Hey There\! account. Additionally, the settings tab is highlighted below to indicate to the user that the settings tab is open. Overall, this settings page works well with highlighting the key location features that users may utilize and clearly explain to the user what each setting does.

### Messages-

For the Messages page, it appears differently compared to the pages shown previously. To start with, the Messages page acts as the message functionality for our app, allowing users to communicate with one another. Firstly, the Messages page displays at the top the user you are talking to, their distance away from you and the common interests you share with them. Just below that, it shows the chat messages that you and the other user are exchanging; your messages will appear on the right side, and the other user’s messages will appear on the left. Finally, we added a dropdown menu in order to choose which friend to chat with. The menu shows the username of the friend and the distance away from you. Moreover, whichever friend you are currently chatting with will be highlighted in the friends menu. Additionally, this dropdown menu acts as a draggable menu, allowing users to move the menu up and down in order to choose a friend to talk to and expand the chatroom. And just like the previous pages, the Messages tab is highlighted below. Overall, this tab provides unique characteristics and easy to use functionality for users to adjust and control how they interact with the app.

### Map-

For the Map page, the middle section shows a map of your surrounding location thanks to the Google API our app uses. In that map section, it will display the map along with you and other users in a certain vicinity to you. To change that vicinity, there is a draggable menu at the top in order to control the searching method to find nearby users. It holds 2 searching options, Radius and Sort By. Radius controls the searching zone to discover nearby users; so for example, if a nearby user is within that 3 mile radius with similar interests to you, they will appear on the map and the other draggable menu, Nearby Users, that we will discuss soon. The second option is Sort By, which has two options for searching, based on either distance or interests. Distance will sort users with at least one common interest to you within your given radius and display that sorted by closest distance to you in the Nearby Users menu. Interests will sort users with your given radius based on the most common interests they have to you, regardless of closest distance. For this prototype, the sort by option is set to distance. Finally, the Nearby Users menu will display all the nearby users in your given radius. If your sort by option is distance, it will place users with the closest distance to you in ascending order. If your sort by option is interests, it will place users with the most common interests to you in ascending order, regardless of distance. Moreover, when you select a nearby user on either the map or in the Nearby Users menu, they will be highlighted on both. Additionally, the Map tab will be highlighted in the very bottom menu. Overall, this Map page showcases many of the important features for finding new people, but is still kept relatively simple and easy to follow just like the previous pages shown before.

In conclusion, these pages all follow a very similar format of simplicity and unity; none diverging or doing something extremely different from the rest. This keeps the app easy to navigate and allows users to easily traverse and control what they will do. This is also supported through the clear labeling of each tab/feature along with highlighting to allow users to know what they are looking at/doing.

# Tab 2

## Part 2\. Heuristic Evaluation

**Visibility of system status** 

- Every page has some form of highlighting or selection indication to clearly tell the user what has been chosen.  
- Location settings will be clearly visible to the user, telling them if their location is on/off in a given area (thanks to blackout zones) or if other settings are turned on/off.  
- Automatic saving of information will be shown to the user.

**Match system words to the real world**

- Natural and simple language used in all pages of the app  
  - Create Account, Log In, Name, Age, Bio, Interests, Location, Distance, Users, Radius, Map, Messages, etc.  
- Logo is a waving hand and relates to the real world experience of greeting someone with waving a hand.  
- Everything that could be confusing to the user is explained in simple terms.

**User control and freedom**

- The entirety of the app is controlled by the user.  
  - Creating an account, logging in, setting up one’s user profile, choosing location settings, setting up blackout zones, finding new users, setting up options to find new users, messaging users, etc.  
- Simple removing/changing options for users such as adding and removing certain blackout zones, easily changing their bio in their profile and/or changing their user searching settings.  
- Choosing exact tabs to access thanks to the bottom tab bar.

**Consistency and standards**

- Built as both an iOS and Android application, meaning that the app will follow each platform’s Human Interface Guidelines conventions for navigation patterns, toggle styles, and modal sheets  
- The UI is designed very similarly to many online apps.  
- The UI is designed very simply and utilizes clear buttons and colors for a simple viewing and navigating experience.  
- Any option that is chosen will be correspondingly highlighted to clearly indicate the user has chosen said option.

**Error prevention**

- If any computer error occurs, it will be clearly notified to the user.  
- The app automatically switches the user’s visibility to Hidden when GPS signal is lost, preventing outdated or inaccurate location data.  
- The system notifies users when filter settings result in zero matches  
- If any changes the user makes to their profile is prohibited by our application (Inappropriate name), the user will be notified about the issue and will be prompted to keep their original choice or choose a new one.  
- If the user attempts to search for other users when their location is turned off, they will be prompted that they are not allowed to do said action and must turn on their location to do so.

**Recognition rather than recall**

- All possible buttons, options and icons represent familiarity/users have seen these things before, allowing for users to recognize things easily.  
- In case of confusion, everything is also labeled or highlighted to not have the user need to recall certain aspects.

**Accelerators**

- Not many accelerators on the app  
- When entering or exiting a blackout zone, the user’s location will be updated to either off or on.  
- For returning users, the app will remember the last-used filter configuration and map location.  
- When re-entering the app without logging out, users will not have to log back into their account.

**Minimalist design**

- UI design should be simplistic and not have any confusing design choices.  
- Users on the map should be small and minimal  
- The map is the core interaction surface and shouldn’t be cluttered  
- Real-time messaging should keep communication light and meetups focused  
- Every option choice should be labeled as either on/off based on indication of highlighting to clearly show the user if a feature or option is turned on or off.   
- The UI shouldn’t have a multitude of different colors and instead follows a small color palette.

**Help users recognize and recover from errors**

- The system should provide error messages that clearly describe the cause of error, affected action, and a resolution.  
- When users have certain location settings applied that stops them from completing certain actions (searching for nearby users when your own location is off), they will be prompted by this issue and be told how to fix it.  
- When location history has no data within the last 24 hours, the message should help the user understand what to do differently: “Location tracking was off during this period. Turn it on before your next meetup.”  
- When interest-tag data fails to load, the system should display an error message and should continue to operate using cached tag data.

**Help and documentation**

- All location settings include an exact description of what the setting does.  
- When a user first creates their account for the first time, they will be guided through how the app works and what each tab does.  
- If users already have an account, but are stuck on the create account page, they can click on the link below the create account button to access the log in page  
- If users don’t have an account, but are stuck on the log in page, they can click on the link below the log in button to access the create account page.
